transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-11-21 11:00 PT
- Duration: ~56 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (ForgeBank Head of AI), Lena Ortiz (Platform Eng), Tom Boudreau (Product)

Summary:
Quick improv-style enablement session focused on: tight messaging for latency/cost tradeoffs, live demo of fallback routing and a canary, and rapid rebuttals to common procurement/security questions. Goal: get AE/SE musicality on the pitch and leave ForgeBank with clear next steps for a pilot.

Topics covered:
- Customer stack & constraints (on prem vs cloud, encryption, context length needs)
- Redwood product shorthand and which offering to pitch (hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)
- Live demo script: fallback to smaller model, KV cache explanation, batching knobs
- Objection handling: SOC2/ISO, KMS, data residency, SLAs
- Competitive framing vs OpenAI/Anthropic/SageMaker endpoints

Action items quick list (captured verbally; details above): Alex to send pricing and security docs; Maya to run and share a short benchmark; Samir to confirm pilot throughput numbers.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: alright everybody, uh welcome to a scrimmage session we wanted to keep this tight 45 to 60 minutes, improv style, try a few rebuttals and run a tiny live demo. Maya you good to jump in on the demo half?
[00:14] Maya Singh: yeah for sure, i'll do a super quick routing/fallback demo then we can do role play. i'm going to share screen now, lemme know if the deck link renders for everyone. (link shared: https://redwood.app/d/demo-scrimmage)
[00:28] Samir Patel: link is visible, thanks.
[00:31] Alex Chen: perfect. quick context Samir: you said ForgeBank needs sub-250ms p50 for certain flows and also wants full audit trail, is that right?
[00:42] Samir: yeah core customer flows need low latency, but we have a batch jobs team that's okay with less strict SLOs. also, encryption at rest and KMS integration are musts because of compliance.
[00:55] Lena Ortiz: and to add we are 80% on GCP, but we do have an air-gapped vault in some regions so private deployment is on the table.
[01:05] Alex: okay clear. Maya, show the routing graphic we use.
[01:10] Maya: (screens) so here's a simple policy: route latencysensitive reqs to Dedicated capacity pinned to a smaller optimized model, otherwise route to hosted higher-capacity models for throughput. if Dedicated is saturated, automatic fallback to an elastic hosted variant or a quantized model. you can see the fallback chain, and we highlight cost per million tokens at each step. note: transcription might read KV cache as K V cash in some exports, disregard that hehe.
[01:35] Tom Boudreau: can you explain the KV cache bit again? i think i heard "K V cash" in an earlier internal note and it confused legal...
[01:42] Maya: yeah totally. KV cache = key-value cache for transformer past states; it prevents re-computing prefix tokens so long conversations are cheaper and faster. in practice the runtime manages cache eviction and you can pin common prefixes. sometimes transcripts garble it as K V cash, which is funny.
[01:58] Alex: cool, we'll demo toggling cache on/off so you can see latency delta.
[02:05] Maya: starting demo: running a 6k token prompt, Dedicated small-llm baseline: p50 ~210ms, p95 ~420ms, hosted high throughput variant p50 ~360ms but cost per token lower. now toggling fallback: when Dedicated saturates, request reroutes to hosted 8-bit quantized variant; you see the latency spike but the request still succeeds, and that preserves availability.
[02:36] Samir: nice. what's the typical tokenization overhead? i.e. do we incur extra cost for the cache warm-up?
[02:45] Maya: warm-up is minimal if you have persistent sessions; cold starts can add ~50-100ms. we recommend prefix caching for flows where you repeat system messages.
[02:55] Alex: okay now role play — Tom you'll play procurement. I'll be AE. Maya you be the SE helping with details. we want to practice the SOC2 / on-prem ask.
[03:05] Tom: sounds good. Procurement: "we need assurances on audit logs and a KMS/HSM integration. do you support customer-managed keys?"
[03:15] Maya: yes, Redwood Private can be deployed in your VPC with a private control plane; we support KMS integrations and HSM workflows. we also produce audit logs per request and support long retention. for hosted, we have envelope encryption and SOC2 attestation; customer-managed keys are available on Private and in some Dedicated packages.
[03:37] Tom: procurement follow-up: "what about data residency, we cannot allow data to leave EU for EU customers"
[03:45] Alex: you can pin model variants and capacity to region-specific clusters, plus Private gives you full control. i'll follow up with our compliance sheet that lists regional deployments.
[03:55] Samir: objection — "why not just run OpenAI and pay the extra cost?"
[04:02] Alex: two answers: economics and control. Redwood Optimize recommendations and automatic batching often reduce unit cost versus naive API calls, and Dedicated gives you predictable throughput at lower marginal cost than unmanaged cloud endpoints. plus you get rollouts and canaries integrated so you avoid silent regressions.
[04:20] Tom: what about latency variance vs Anthropic? we see some variance in benchmarks.
[04:25] Maya: latency varies by model architecture and region. our kernel selection and continuous batching reduce tail latency; we can run a head-to-head with your sample workload. i'll schedule a benchmark and demonstrate p50/p95 under realistic concurrency.
[04:40] Alex: quick note on risk: for regulated flows we often recommend Private, but for rapid time-tomarket many customers start hosted and move to Dedicated as throughput solidifies.
[04:52] Samir: okay makes sense. let's try another rapid-fire objection: security folks ask about remote code execution vector in function calling.
[05:00] Maya: for function calling, Redwood enforces a sandboxed runner and role-based access to tools; you can whitelist allowed endpoints and have audit trails for actions invoked by model outputs. we also allow request-level policies to disable certain capabilities.
[05:18] Alex: we got a question in chat about on-prem packaging — are there size or GPU constraints?
[05:24] Lena: yes curious about min cluster size for Private.
[05:28] Maya: minimum configuration depends on model family. for mid-size models we recommend at least 4x A100-equivalent nodes for redundancy and cache performance; smaller models can run on 2 nodes but you'll trade throughput. we'll share a sizing guide.
[05:42] Alex: alright, improv pivot — i will simulate pricing pushback: "we can't commit to Dedicated, price is too high." Maya, what are quick levers?
[05:49] Maya: levers: reduce model size, enable aggressive quantization (8-bit/4-bit where acceptable), tune batching parameters, and use prefix caching. also pluggable fallbacks keep SLAs while you save cost. we can show cost-per-response charts.
[06:05] Tom: can we get per-route cost breakdowns?
[06:09] Alex: yes Redwood Console has token-level cost and per-route dashboards; we'll include screenshots.
[06:15] (short crosstalk, Alex types link into chat)
[06:20] Alex: moving to rebuttal practice — i'll play a skeptical engineer and Tom you be the vendor. start with "we already built an LLM wrapper in house"
[06:29] Tom: "we already built an LLM wrapper in house so why do we buy Redwood?"
[06:32] Maya: you can keep the wrapper for orchestration, but Redwood provides production runtime optimizations: kernel selection, KV cache management, automatic batching, and a predictable path to lowest marginal cost. plus, we maintain the operational burden — upgrades, rollback, tracing, and incident response.
[06:48] Samir: follow-up: "how do we validate model quality doesn't regress on a new bundle?"
[06:53] Maya: Redwood Optimize offers eval hooks — you pin prompt suites and get regression alerts tied to quality thresholds. we also support canary rollouts so a small percent of traffic hits the new model first.
[07:05] Alex: quick demo clip — Maya, show the canary rollout config and how the Console shows a drop in a metric.
[07:12] Maya: (narrates) here is the console screenshot: you configure canary at route level, pick metric baseline, choose failover policy (auto rollback if quality drops > X%), and schedule. console triggers trace ids for failing requests so you can debug.
[07:28] Tom: do you have customers using this in finance?
[07:31] Alex: yes, a regional bank used canary + auto rollback when they updated system prompts; it prevented a noisy hallucination from going wide.
[07:38] Samir: okay last improv round: "we require a POC that runs in VPC and ingests 5k reqs/min for 2 weeks. what's the minimal path?"
[07:47] Maya: I'd propose a two-phase POC: 1) Hosted quick validation with sample data to prove latency and quality in 1 week, 2) Dedicated reserved capacity pilot in your VPC for scale test. we can provide a sizing doc and a short runbook.
[08:02] Alex: let's capture next steps now...
[08:06] (quick recap)
[08:08] Alex: recap: Alex sends pricing + security docs; Maya runs bench and shares demo clip; Samir to confirm target throughput and timeline for pilot. we'll reconvene after materials are shared.
[08:20] Tom: thanks, this was helpful. small note — transcription sometimes changes Redwood product names (e.g., Redwood Optimize -> "red wood optimize") in automated exports, just flagging for the notes.
[08:31] Maya: noted.
[08:33] Alex: any final questions?
[08:36] Samir: none right now, thanks team.
[08:39] Alex: great, end of session.

(End of recording — remaining minutes used to confirm links in chat and type follow-ups)

Notes on quality: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings (K V cache vs KV cache, redwood product name splits, numerical latencies sometimes truncated), marked as medium quality.
